reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / NCCN & genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused by germline variants in the tumour suppressor gene STK11 (LKB1), inherited autosomal dominantly, with a proportion arising de novo
Characterised by mucocutaneous pigmented macules, typically on the lips, perioral skin, buccal mucosa, and digits, which often fade in adulthood
Hallmark lesions are hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract, most numerous in the small bowel
Small-bowel polyps commonly cause recurrent intussusception, obstruction, and bleeding, often presenting in childhood or adolescence
Confers a markedly increased lifetime risk of a broad range of cancers, including gastrointestinal (colorectal, gastric, small bowel, pancreatic), breast, and gynaecological tumours

Distinctive gynaecological associations include ovarian sex cord tumours with annular tubules and cervical adenoma malignum, and males may develop testicular Sertoli cell tumours causing gynaecomastia

Management combines surveillance and elective polypectomy (including intraoperative enteroscopy) to reduce complications, with the aim of clearing significant small-bowel polyps and avoiding repeated emergency resections
Multi-organ cancer surveillance spanning the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, breast, and reproductive organs is required from early adulthood
reference.pathophysiology: STK11 encodes a serine-threonine kinase that regulates cell polarity, energy metabolism, and growth through the AMPK-mTOR pathway, acting as a tumour suppressor. Loss of STK11 function disrupts these controls, producing disorganised hamartomatous overgrowth of the intestinal mucosa and predisposing multiple epithelial tissues to malignant transformation. The mucocutaneous pigmentation reflects abnormal melanocyte activity associated with the same genetic defect.
additionalDifferentials: Cowden syndrome and other PTEN hamartoma tumour syndromes
Laugier-Hunziker syndrome (benign mucocutaneous pigmentation without polyps)
additionalInvestigations: Germline STK11 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis with genetic counselling
Small-bowel surveillance with video capsule endoscopy or magnetic resonance enterography
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy with polypectomy
Breast imaging and pancreatic surveillance (e.g. MRI or endoscopic ultrasound) from early adulthood
Gynaecological assessment and testicular examination for the characteristic gonadal tumours
redFlags: Acute intussusception or small-bowel obstruction from a large hamartomatous polyp
Significant or recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia
Precocious puberty or gynaecomastia suggesting a hormonally active gonadal tumour
New pancreatic, breast, or gynaecological symptoms given the high multi-organ cancer risk
reference.prognosis: The cumulative lifetime cancer risk across multiple organs is high, and gastrointestinal complications contribute substantial morbidity from childhood onward. Structured surveillance, elective polyp clearance, and early cancer detection improve outcomes, but lifelong multidisciplinary follow-up is necessary.
pitfalls: Dismissing perioral pigmentation as cosmetic and missing the underlying diagnosis
Repeated emergency bowel resections leading to short-bowel syndrome instead of planned polyp clearance with enteroscopy
Concentrating on the gut and overlooking pancreatic, breast, and gynaecological cancer risk
Assuming pigmentation persists lifelong, since it can fade in adults and be absent in relatives
